newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian election launches new post-Communist era.
newsitem.headline: Romanian election launches new post-Communist era.

text.p: Romania embarked on a new era of post-Communist reform on Monday after Emil Constantinescu's presidential election triumph over the man who had led the East European country since its bloody upheaval in 1989.

Exit polls gave Constantinescu a seven or eight point margin over ex-Communist Ion Iliescu, reviled by liberals as the man who hobbled real reforms after coming to power in the aftermath of Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's execution.

"We are here to say that Romania will become once again the dignified and prosperous country we all wanted," Constantinescu told tens of thousands of people from the balcony over University Square, where the first shootings occurred in the December 1989 revolution.

Constantinescu, who turns 57 on Tuesday, has the immediate task of forming a government. The geology professor told his supporters they were "home again because in this square we conquered liberty. This square is kilometre zero of democracy in Romania".
That was a reference to a 1990 address he made from the same spot to student protesters. They were dispersed by miners' riots which he and other liberals say were incited by Iliescu.
Revellers embraced, cracked open champagne and swayed to disco music in the square. Cars raced up and down boulevards tooting horns well into the night.
Mass celebrations were held in Timisoara, where the 1989 revolution started, and other provincial towns.
The outcome reversed the result of the 1992 election in which Iliescu easily defeated Constantinescu in a run-off.
It also ended Romania's status as the sole East European state where former communists had yet to be dislodged.
"It is the first time in Romania's history that a leader is departing in a democratic way," commentator Ion Cristoiu told commercial television.
"Not strangled, not in a coup, not shot in Tirgoviste (Ceausescu's execution). That is why today is an historic day."
Iliescu was contrite, conceding defeat without even seeing official results. He pledged to form a constructive opposition.
"Let us learn the lessons of the Olympic movement," he said. "Whether you win or lose, you carry on."

For Constantinescu, the victory amounted to a green light to proceed with faster reforms after his Democratic Convention (CDR) threw Iliescu's leftist party out of government in parliamentary polls earlier this month.
"The time for action has begun. From this moment, we'll have to work," he told a television interviewer.
"We will have an austerity programme. We have an extremely difficult legacy. The government must apply long-term reform but must achieve results quickly."
During the bitter election campaign Constantinescu accused Iliescu of seven years of corrupt mismanagement that had left Romanians in poverty with average monthly salaries of less than $100.

Iliescu had tried to persuade voters to stick by his cautious approach to reforms. He had said a victory for Constantinescu would prompt mass sackings of ex-Communists and bring back pre-Second World War landlords bent on reclaiming homes.
Constantinescu pledged there would be no retribution but promised to shed light on questions from the past raised during the campaign -- including 1,200 unexplained deaths during the 1989 revolution.
"I guarantee there will be no cleansing here," he said. "There will be no political trials. I will do nothing to start a political vendetta, but the truth must be known."
